utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, to continue with your examination-in-chief. Would you let me know how much longer you will be with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter was on the wrong channel and apologises, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please start again, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, looking at my notes, Mr. Robinson, I think I will need these three days of this week to complete my examination of Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Seselj, please bear two things in mind, the interpreters: don't speak too fast, and don't speak too loud. Yes, start, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we heard Mr. Nice allege that the goal of what was happening was the expansion of territory. Tell me, please, since you were in the Krajina, in Bosnia, did the Serbs in Krajina and Bosnia respond to the threats they were facing with a view to enlarging their territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is absolutely not so. The Serbs were responding to the unlawful toppling of the constitutional order. The constitutional order of the then Yugoslavia did not permit the secession of federal units. In the general principles of the constitution, there was the right of nations to self-determination, and it was felt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop a minute, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if I might just express a view of what's happening here, because I'm concerned that another three days are going to be taken by this examination-in-chief, which I doubt very much is in Mr. Milosevic's own best interests. That was a very simple question, which you've answered already, and you now embark on telling us about the constitutional order, which you've told us about several times already, as have many other witnesses. I ask you to reflect on whether this kind of answer is of any use to the Chamber, which has heard it so often already, when it's a factual matter you were asked about and you were able to give a very simple answer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask another question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will put a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in response to one of my questions you said that when you visited the Krajina you personally saw barricades, you saw the situation on the ground. Were barricades erected in the Krajina in order to expand the territory or to protect the people from the threat they were facing? Please give us a very specific reply. What were the threats they were facing when they erected barricades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I regret that the Chamber did not submit to me on time a list of desirable responses. Then I could respond in the way you want me to. Secondly, my responses are my own opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is utter impertinence. I would invite you to show some respect when you're dealing with questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am showing you the utmost respect but you are not showing respect to me as a witness. I don't know why you are so nervous and angry. That is unfitting for a Judge. I have never expressed anger or nervousness here, Mr. Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, just answer the question and let us -- let us get on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs on the territory of the Croatian federal unit felt existentially threatened. The newly set-up Tudjman regime abolished their status as a constituent nation. They revived old Ustasha fascist symbols and immediately started persecuting the Serbian population. The Serbs had a strong historical memory of World War II and the genocide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have answered the question. Next question. We don't want a rehash of evidence that has already been given, Mr. Milosevic. That is not a profitable use of the Court's time. Move to an area that you have not yet dealt with. You have dealt with these matters already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We will not now go into the constitutional changes that were made to their detriment, but at that time was it very clear or was it only a vague threat to the existence of the Serbs on their territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were numerous incidents in which Serbs were victims. Let me remind you of the case of Miroslav Mlinar from Benkovci who was unlawfully arrested and beaten up, and he barely survived the beating. There were innumerable such instances all over the Croatian federal unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. You have answered the question. You have said that there were numerous incidents, so that in your view it was not merely vague. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, then, was this defence of their own homes and villages rather than an expansion of territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were defending their homes and villages. In villages on the Croatian territorial unit where the Serbs were in the majority, the mayors and the chiefs of police were Serbs. Most Serbs were members of the police. On several occasions, Croatian special purpose policemen entered these places to steal weapons from the police stations for -- to make sure that the police in these villages did not have any serious weapons. This was a cause of dissatisfaction among the Serbs and the direct conflicts between the Serb population and the Croatian special purpose policemen. There were many places where this happened, and this culminated in the events in Pakrac in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did these conflicts show any intention on the part of the Serbs to enlarge their territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Serbs simply showed no interest in controlling territory on which they were not the majority population. They didn't want any kind of splitting up of the Croatian federal unit either but, feeling existentially threatened, they were simply preventing Croatian special purpose policemen bearing Ustasha fascist insignia from taking control over their villages and towns, bearing in mind their experiences in World War II when something similar happened and when a genocide was perpetrated over the Serb people and they were killed en masse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us now consider Bosnia and Herzegovina. Were there any reasons that might lead one to conclude that the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina were responding to the problems they were facing with a view to enlarging their territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two reasons: First, the Muslim political leadership established the so-called Patriotic League, and this Patriotic League established its own paramilitary organisation, the so-called Green Berets. This was done long before the onset of the civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Secondly, there had already been numerous incidents. One of these occurred around the 1st of March, 1992. There was a Serb wedding in the old Serb church in Sarajevo, several hundred years old, one of the oldest Serbian churches in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was a Serb wedding going on and a group of Muslims on that occasion killed the groom's father, Nikola Gajdovic. This is something that alarmed Serbs all over Bosnia and Herzegovina and made them realise what was in store for them because in World War II part of the Muslims were allies of the Croatian Ustasha fascist regime and participated in its paramilitary organisations in the Ustasha movement which represented the Croatian version of the SS troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Generally, as a rule of thumb, I am not going to allow any answer that exceeds four or five sentences. As a general rule. I will exercise my discretion. Mr. Milosevic, I urge you to move from the general to the specific. It's not -- it's not merely a question of whether the Serbs had something to respond to, as this question and answer indicates. What is of more relevance is whether any of these responses on the parts of the Serbs related to any of the incidents in the indictment. So I urge you to concentrate on that. Move from the general to the specific. We know what -- as a general, what your case is, but let us see whether you have evidence that will challenge the specific incidents alleged in the indictment. Yes, next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I am bearing in mind one of the main theses presented by Mr. Nice, which is that the intention was to enlarge territory. I want to show that this is absolute nonsense. Mr. Nice's allegation is absolute nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, are you aware of the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did the Serbs accept this plan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbs accepted Cutileiro's plan and this plan was drawn up following the instructions of the then European Community, and it was based on a territorial division of Bosnia and Herzegovina into three cantons based on the ethnic make-up of the population according to the census of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, are you aware of the fact that, according to the Cutileiro Plan, the Serbs were to get about 44 per cent of the territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. I don't know whether it was 43 or 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So they accepted a smaller territory than they were later granted by the Dayton Accord.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody accepted it; Serbs, Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To go back to this question, is this something that shows that they had no intention of enlarging their territory? They accepted what the European Commission offered them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop. That's a leading question. That's a leading question. It's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you said they accepted 44 per cent. What was your attitude to the Cutileiro Plan? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally supported the plan, as did the Serb Radical Party to which I belonged. We advocated a solution whereby the Serbs would keep their status as a constituent nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina whether Bosnia and Herzegovina remained in Yugoslavia or not. So what mattered was the status of a constituent nation. However, immediately after the adoption of the Cutileiro Plan, the European Community unilaterally recognised independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and right after that the Muslims reneged on the Cutileiro Plan. On the 18th of March, 1992, the Cutileiro Plan was adopted and as soon as the 6th of April, on the anniversary of the bombing of Belgrade by Hitler in World War II, the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised. What a strange coincidence. And then the Muslims no longer wanted the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, what do you know about the attitude of other political parties and groups in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina to this plan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no political party or institution rejected the Cutileiro Plan until the Muslims rejected it after the proclamation of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Something else happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as around the 18th of March, it was adopted by all sides - I mean the Cutileiro Plan - the Serbs and Muslims began giving up control over police stations in places that belonged to one or the other canton. But as soon as the Muslims turned their backs on the Cutileiro Plan, they tried to get some of these police stations back by force, police stations they had handed over to the Serbs because they were on territory that was to belong to a Serb canton, and that's where incidents occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I anticipate that very soon the interpreters are going to be asking for you to slow down. Observe the pause between question and answer. And you are speaking too fast, Mr. Seselj. Continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In one of your replies you mentioned the establishment of the Patriotic League and the military organisation of the Muslims, the purpose of which was to take part in armed hostilities. Do you know that the 31st of March, 1991, the date a full year before the armed clashes, is still a holiday in the federation part of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the day of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me what your standpoint was with regard to the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Radical Party and I personally opposed the adoption of the Vance-Owen Plan. You supported this plan as the president of the Republic of Serbia. It was also supported by the authorities in Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but it was rejected by the Republika Srpska. We opposed it because, according to that plan, Bosnia and Herzegovina would be divided into nine cantons and Sarajevo would have a special status as a separate cantonal district. Three cantons were to have a Serb majority, three a Croat majority, and three a Muslim majority. The problem for the Serbs was that there was no territorial contiguity between these cantons. This was unacceptable to the Serbs. The Vance-Owen Plan later caused fierce fighting between the Croats and the Muslims because in three cantons the Muslims -- or, rather, the Croats, although they numbered 17 per cent, got 25 per cent of the territory. In three Croatian cantons, the Serbs did not have the absolute majority but only a relative majority. So they hastened to expel from these territories their former allies, the Muslims, because they wanted to have territory where they would be in the majority. And this led to an even more fierce war in Bosnia and Herzegovina than the one that had previously been waged between the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you said that Republika Srpska also refused that plan. Do you remember that Radovan Karadzic first accepted and signed that plan at negotiations in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did sign but under certain conditions. In fact, his acceptance was conditional, pending the approval of the Assembly. The Assembly rejected the plan at a session that you attended as well as Dobrica Cosic, then president of Yugoslavia, and the Prime Minister of Greece, Mitsotakis. You tried to persuade Serb deputies to accept the plan, but they didn't listen to you and rejected it. I think it was definitively rejected at the following session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you know about the attitude of other political parties and factors in the FRY to the Vance-Owen Plan? You explained the position of this Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbia only the Socialist Party of Serbia accepted it. All the other parties - the Democratic Party, the Serb Renewal Movement, and the Serb Radical Party and all the others - rejected the Vance-Owen Plan, and you can see that from the attempt to hold a pan-Serb Assembly in May 1992 that was supposed to be attended by all deputies of the FRY, of the Republic of Serbia, of Montenegro, Republika Srpska, and Serbian Krajina. The organisers had meant to exert pressure on the deputies of the Assembly of Republika Srpska to accept the plan. However, all the parties in Serbia refused even to attend, except the Serb Radical Party which attended, but at the session we attacked the plan and then we walked out. And without us, the other participants were left without a quorum, so the Federal Assembly was unable to adopt a valid decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what position did you take on the conflict between the authorities of the FRY and Republika Srpska that ensued?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire Radical Party and myself sided with the authorities of Republika Srpska, opposing you and all the authorities in the FRY. First of all, we held a protest rally in Loznica, and then I went to Knezina, and I gathered the most prominent military commanders of the Serb army who were members of the Radical Party, I proclaimed them dukes of the Radical Party, and I supported the Assembly of Republika Srpska in their rejection of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you the only ones who did so?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody did the same. Zoran Djindjic or, rather, the Democratic Party of which he was vice-president. The president was still Dragoljub Micunovic. The Serbian Renewal Movement had a lot of reservations. They did not exactly support the authorities of Republika Srpska but they were also against your authorities and against every position you took. I can't remember the details of their public statements from the time, but in any case, your Socialist Party and the authorities controlled by the Socialist Party were the only ones who supported the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on, can you clarify something for me. One of the answers, or part of the answer you have just given has been translated, "I gathered the most prominent military commanders of the Serb army who were members of the Radical Party, I proclaimed them dukes of the Radical Party." Could you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a problem of your interpreters, Mr. Bonomy. I proclaimed them Serb Chetnik dukes, according to the old Serb tradition. The most senior in title Serb Chetnik duke is entitled to bestow that title on other -- on others, to proclaim them dukes. And I bestowed that title on them for their military contribution. They were not really high-ranking commanders. They commanded up to one company, but they were prominent fighters. I don't know whether you know this: The only living Serb Chetnik vojvoda, duke, Momcilo Djuic, who lived in America, proclaimed me duke in 1989 - that was a long time before the war - in order to preserve the tradition, because if he had died before proclaiming me duke, the tradition could not have been preserved. And I in my turn proclaimed 19 or 20 new Chetnik dukes. I can't remember. I don't remember many of their names. Among those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's an adequate explanation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note Mr. Seselj speaks too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, did you hear that? The interpreters say that you speak too fast. Can you do something about that? It's within your power.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I keep trying, Mr. Robinson, but sometimes I get carried away in my answer. It is quite spontaneous, completely spontaneous, I assure you, but I'll keep trying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, what was your attitude toward the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, the Serb Radicals, accepted that plan. We supported it. It was also supported by all parties in Serbia. It was accepted by the leadership of Republika Srpska. However, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan was rejected by the Muslim leadership. That plan was relatively good. It proceeded from the premise that the three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina were constituent peoples, that they have under their respective controls cantons or provinces or entities, whatever you want to call them. I don't remember what they were called in the plan itself. And according to that plan, I believe that Republika Srpska got a little over 45 per cent of the territory. However, the Muslims rejected that plan because they did not want any plan that divided Bosnia and Herzegovina into three entities. That plan envisaged the structuring of Bosnia and Herzegovina as something between a federation and a confederation, and in some of its aspects that plan coincided with the Dayton Accords that came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that the main reason for rejecting that plan was that the three peoples were placed on an equal footing?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explain how the plan was scuttled by the rejection of the Muslim side. What was the attitude of the Contact Group? What was your attitude to the plan of the Contact Group?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had our reservations towards that plan because it wanted Republika Srpska to give up in advance one-third of its territory or, rather, the territory that was held by the Serb army. That was over 70 per cent of the entire territory. That was supposed to be reduced to 49 per cent without any political arrangement attached. That was the most problematic aspect of it in our eyes. We thought that 49 per cent was otherwise good for the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, economically speaking, they were less valuable territories, and the third problem was to how to persuade Serb people living outside that chunk of territory to move and go and live somewhere else. That was the main problem faced by the authorities of Republika Srpska. So the plan of the Contact Group did not guarantee a final political solution that would be convenient to the Serb people, but it wanted, nevertheless, the leadership of Republika Srpska to agree to the reduction of their territory to 49 per cent. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What knowledge do you have about the attitude of other political parties and groups in Yugoslavia to the Contact Group Plan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, if I remember correctly, your plan -- that plan was unanimously supported by your party. I believe Draskovic supported it as well. However, democratic parties rejected that plan as well, as did the Serb Radical Party for the reasons I already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What position did you take then with the increasing tensions between the authorities of the FRY and the leadership of Republika Srpska that resulted from their rejection of the Contact Group Plan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was 1995. The relationship was already very strained. The power held by your party personified by you already imposed a blockade of Republika Srpska and banned any crossing of the border to Republika Srpska. The blockade had been introduced even earlier, but it became even stronger in 1995. You even brought international observers to monitor the blockade, because you stated that the blockade itself was not sufficient, that it was being violated. So your party, your authorities brought international observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This step we took, was that a kind of pressure to accept the Contact Group Plan and continue negotiations?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a form of pressure of the FRY authorities --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... however subtly expressed. If the accused wishes to explain the objective of the course he then took, he can give evidence about it. If he's not going to give evidence, he can't put the proposition to a witness. While I'm on feet can I just say a couple of things. First of all, the Prosecution doesn't accept at all that this witness is incapable of speaking either slowly or in a moderate volume, and it is extremely difficult to follow his evidence and it's our respectful submission to the Court that he shows insufficient respect either to the Court or indeed to the interpreters who I know have considerable difficulty with interpreting what he says. The second thing I observe is that although this material can't be said to be wholly irrelevant, a great deal of it's been covered in other ways already through other witnesses in cross-examination or in reports or in evidence in chief of one kind or another, and I'd ask the Chamber to have in mind that if this accused takes six days in chief with this witness, he will have been expending a significant portion of the remaining time presently allotted to him for his Defence case, and I just make it clear now, as I made it clear earlier by implication, that any and every application for an extension of time that may be made by this accused will be resisted by the Prosecution, because it is quite clear that he has not made the best use of his time. And my last point is that this material, if it was valuable, and it's clearly well-prepared in the sense that short questions bring long answers that seem to forecast the questions maybe, if this material is valuable, it should have been and could have been in written form. But I would invite the Chamber to require this witness to speak more slowly and at a lower volume so that we can deal with him more easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, as to the last matter raised by the Prosecution, I have said to you time and again that you are speaking too fast and you are speaking far too loudly. I regret to say that, in my view, it reflects a kind of emotional insecurity, this need to speak so fast and so loudly. Why is it necessary? It's a matter within your control. It creates difficulty for the interpreters, and therefore it affects the efficiency of the Court if every five or ten minutes the interpreters have to be asking you to speak more slowly and less loudly. Mr. Milosevic, the question that you asked was obviously leading. Rephrase it, and bear in mind the time that is allotted to you, and ask yourself the question do you need to spend this amount of time with this witness? Because that is going to be taken into consideration when you make, as you have said you will, an application for an extension of time when the 150 days have expired. Instead of spending another three days with this witness, in my estimation you could spend two and be as productive and as effective. Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I do bear in mind that Mr. Seselj is an authentic witness of very important events, in fact all the key events in the territories of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I will rephrase my question. The introduction of that embargo was certainly a very painful measure. Tell me, why did we opt for that measure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I have to strenuously protest because of the psychiatric qualification of emotional insecurity that Mr. Robinson gave to my testimony. I believe that is extremely inappropriate because, in psychiatry, Mr. Robinson, this qualification has a very negative connotation. I speak this way -- I've always spoken this way. I cannot adjust to your expectations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have stopped you. I've stopped you. I've allowed you to comment on my qualification, my characterisation. I think you have the right to. You have commented on it. Now, whether that may be so or not, it is in the interest of Mr. Milosevic and of everybody here, Mr. Seselj, for you to speak more softly and not as fast as you have. Never mind my characterisation. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to answer the question asked by Mr. Milosevic. I still remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very focused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. The question that he asked was a leading question, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you've given me the floor in order to answer. I have taken the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "The introduction of that embargo was certainly a very painful measure." And, "Why did we opt for that measure?" A comment very, very briefly on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That measure was adopted by the authorities in the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia because the Western powers, since in their view the leadership of Republika Srpska was intransigent, always moved the pressure on to Belgrade and insisted that Mr. Milosevic should always be an intermediary between the Western powers and the leadership of Republika Srpska. They asked him to support every one of their alleged peace efforts, and so on and so forth. As for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, very serious sanctions were imposed on the country by the Western powers, saying that they were not supportive enough of peace efforts, and the government and the authorities in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and in the Republic of Serbia had no control over the authorities of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. What was your view or what is your view now of the Dayton agreement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Radical Party was against the Dayton agreement for several reasons. First of all, in principle we could have agreed to reduce Republika Srpska to 49 per cent of the territory of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What's the relevance for this trial of this witness or his party's views on Dayton? If there is relevance, I shall listen to the evidence with interest, but for the life of me I can't immediately see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Dayton agreement was a landmark. It marked the end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Dayton agreement established Republika Srpska and the Muslim-Croat federation. It is very important to know how big its value was and what the position was of political factors in Yugoslavia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the Dayton agreement. Mr. Seselj said that his party had a negative attitude. Now I want to ask him the following: Since the Dayton agreement for the Serb side was more favourable than the Cutileiro Plan, I'm asking him to explain. I'm not asking him. He is not the one who is answering here, he's not the one who is accused here. I want him to answer why they had a negative attitude towards the Cutileiro Plan and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Milosevic. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, it is relevant. Give us your answer briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serb Radical Party led the political front of rejecting the Dayton agreement in Serbia. We were followed in this by the Democratic Party and the Democratic Party of Serbia. We were against the Dayton agreement because Republika Srpska did not -- remained landlocked and therefore did not have any access to the sea although this had been promised in the region of Debelo Brdo, behind Cavtat. Also, there was no guaranteed territorial link between the western and the eastern part of Republika Srpska because the Serbs had to leave all of Sarajevo, even Grbavica, because the status of Brcko was left to be resolved later in a very perfidious way, through so-called international arbitration. It was said that the inter-ethnic boundary line in the area of Brcko or the district of Brcko would be resolved by arbitration. However, this was a big-time deception because all of Brcko was taken out of Republika Srpska and proclaimed an independent district in order not to have any link between the eastern and western part of Republika Srpska and in a future crisis the western part would completely be cut off. Those were our reasons. Today, the Serb Radical Party is fighting tooth and nail for preserving the Dayton agreement because the international governors of Bosnia-Herzegovina have already seriously trampled upon the provisions of the Dayton agreement in order to turn Bosnia-Herzegovina into a unitary state. According to the Dayton agreement, it is the entities that are in charge of their respective armies. Now a single army has been proclaimed. Now they are trying to seize the police force of Republika Srpska. There is destruction of entities that is taking on -- taking place now. So that the Serbs and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be held hostage by the international efforts not to create a Muslim state in the middle of Europe. So now we Serbs are twofold victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand this. Are you ascribing these weaknesses now to the Dayton agreement or to the violence exerted over the Dayton agreement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what our position was at the time of the adoption of the Dayton agreement, but now it is the international factors who are supposed to safeguard and implement the Dayton agreement that are violating it the most. That is the danger looming over the Serb people. And also there are systematic threats against the leadership of Republika Srpska. There are even some individual threats that some of them will find themselves in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The Hague if they do not bow to international ultimatums, especially the international governor of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now it is Paddy Ashdown. Before that it was Westendorf, and then that Austrian whatever his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now that we're talking about the Dayton agreement, Mr. Seselj, is it possible to take any step in order to change the Dayton agreement without the consent of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to delve into here. Move on to another subject matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you mentioned the time when we first met, when we first talked. Let us now look at the actual time frame, but I'm interested in the contents too, the first, second, third meeting. These talks of ours in terms of their timing and their substance, how do they fit into this thesis of a criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They absolutely cannot fit into this thesis of a criminal enterprise because we had periods of cooperation --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... prepared. What the Chamber might be assisted by is evidence of fact about the meetings and then it's up to the Chamber ultimately to decide whether things fit or not into a thesis of a criminal enterprise. But I must say questions of this form, especially when they draw responsive answers, seem to have about them a characterisation of preparation and expectation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Chamber is not going to be helped by hearing evidence of how talks between Mr. Seselj and yourself fit into the thesis of a criminal enterprise. Move Mr. Seselj to evidence that relates to the indictment. General questions and general answers are not going to be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I don't understand this explanation given by Mr. Nice that the questions and answers were rehearsed. I don't see what he's trying to say by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will not go into that at all. I'm not concerned about that. I am concerned about whether the question that you have asked is relevant, whether it is going to be of assistance to the Chamber. As formulated, it's not going to be helpful. Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, let us deal with this on a factual basis completely. What did we talk about during those years throughout the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is what did you talk about -- we are not interested in what you and Mr. Seselj spoke about. Relate it to some specific matter in the indictment. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, my colleagues see what you are getting at, but you haven't put the question the right way, because you may elicit an answer that you talked about social matters. We're not interested in that. There is an allegation that Mr. Seselj, yourself, and others were members of a joint criminal enterprise, so it may be relevant to hear what kind of discussions you had that might have related to that, but in the manner that you have formulated it, you may get any kind of answer. So I want the question reformulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, when did we meet, and what topics did we discuss?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, the first meeting was in May 1992, when we talked about the coming federal elections. The second meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Pause there for a second, Mr. Seselj. In May 1992, when we talked about the coming federal elections, was the topic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, or any other such topic raised except for this particular subject, the federal elections?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No other topics were discussed. The meeting took place for about an hour or two, I cannot remember exactly, but it was devoted in its entirety to the fact that, according to the instructions given by foreign embassies in Belgrade and foreign intelligence agencies, Western political parties refused to take part in federal elections. So it was only the Serb Radical Party and your Socialist Party that were prepared to take part in the federal elections. You wanted to hear my opinion, and you wanted to hear whether my party would boycott the elections or not. Then I told you about what we knew as to what the Western foreign intelligence agencies were doing, and we said that we would take part in the elections because we did recognise the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which was proclaimed on the 27th of April that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the influence of those parties that boycotted the elections, in view of the fact that it is the citizens who are voting in the elections?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: By an overwhelming majority the citizens voted in that election, and the Serb Radical Party at these federal elections won about one-third of the parliamentary seats in the area of Serbia and we won three parliamentary seats in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This meeting of ours in May 1992 -- that's when it took place, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It pertained to the federal elections in the FRY. When did we next meet, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember most of them and with a considerable degree of exactitude. The next meeting was after the elections, when you called me and suggested to me that we put up Dobrica Cosic as a candidate for the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, although earlier on your Socialist Party and the Democratic Party of Socialists of Montenegro were in favour of Svetozar Marovic [phoen] whereas the Radicals were in favour of Branko Kostic. You then told me of your proposal about Dobrica Cosic, and I agreed. But you told me that Dobrica Cosic did not want to be a candidate of political parties but of the Association of Serbs from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina respectively. And that's how this was done, and this was accepted by our party and the Montenegrins later on as well. Our next contact had to do with the candidacy of Milan Panic as federal Prime Minister. Milan Panic was an American businessman from California. Our public already knew about him through the privatisation of the Galenika company. It was a Saturday, I remember that very well. You sent someone from the Presidency of Serbia at 11.00 in the evening to see me and to tell me to come. An offer was made to me to sign a public press release that you had already signed as well as Vlajko Stojiljkovic as then-president of the Chamber of Commence of the Republic of Serbia, that we together propose Milan Panic as a candidate. Until then I hadn't heard anything bad about Milan Panic. I thought that he was a Serb patriot from the far-away California. I agreed in principle, I signed the press release, and already by the following morning it was all over the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any other one of our meetings, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was yet another meeting that year, when I was trying to persuade you that we should overthrow Milan Panic in the Federal Assembly and you had many critical remarks as well. However, at that time you did not want your party to take part in his overthrow so at the initiative of the Serb Radical Party there was a vote and only we the Serb Radicals voted in favour of his overthrow. By the following vote you -- your party also voted along with us. It was a decision taken by the leader of your party in parliament but I assumed you agreed to it as well. Our next meeting was after the December 1993 elections. I think it was the beginning of 1994 in actual fact then. We talked about the new federal Prime Minister at the time, you as president of the Socialist Party of Serbia and I, president of the Serb Radical Party, although in addition to that you were president of the Republic of Serbia. Our position was that Milan Panic cannot remain federal Prime Minister by any means, and our party had already voted on a no-confidence vote for him and in favour of Radoje Kontic from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you've dealt with 1992, 1993, and 1994 now.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we're dealing with 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in December 1992 that the elections took place, so our next meeting had to do with the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the Vance-Owen Plan. You've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just remind you of another meeting. The last time when you tried to persuade me to accept the Vance-Owen Plan it was at the state villa in Boticeva Street. You called me, I came, you tried to persuade me, and that took a long time but you didn't manage to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's 1993.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That subject was to stop the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The subject was the Vance-Owen Plan. You were trying to convince me of all the advantages of that plan. I was opposed to it, and I was presenting my arguments against the plan, and we could not reach agreement in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since the topic was Bosnia in the broadest sense, this topic or, rather, this discussion of ours about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, can that be brought into the context of any kind of joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that the Vance-Owen Plan was a peace initiative, not a criminal initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's inappropriate, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And further, Mr. Seselj, is there anything more to say about our meetings?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had another encounter, as far as I can recall, in early September 1993. The Serb Radical Party had moved to initiate the replacement of the government headed by Nikola Sainovic. We had supported that minority government for about six months. You tried to convince me not to have the government dismissed. You proposed various forms of the economic programme. However, our relations were so disrupted because of the Vance-Owen Plan that we failed to reach an agreement and very soon there was a fierce conflict between our two political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is all you can say about our meetings?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no further meetings until 1997. Our first next meeting was in 1997 when you were elected president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We, the Serb Radicals, had voted against you, but after you were elected we attended a reception that you organised in the Federal Assembly building on the occasion of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So through all of these contacts of ours - I want to avoid putting Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a leading question - how was the problem of the civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina treated?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You continually supported every peace initiative. My party supported some and rejected others. The Cutileiro Plan or the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan were plans where we saw eye-to-eye more or less. However, when it came to the Dayton agreement, we were on quite different wavelengths, so one cannot say that we had a unified approach or a unified standpoint. We, the Serb Radicals, opposed in principle to Western interference in our internal affairs on the Balkans because we never trusted the Western powers. We always felt they were trying to dupe us, to trick us, that they were trying to do damage to the Serb people, and you were always willing to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I hope we have clarified the relationship between these alleged participants in the so-called joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because let me remind you that this was only with relation to the so-called Croatian indictment. However, in the Bosnian indictment some names are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where does the difference lie between the two indictments?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the names of the officials of Republika Srpska and the Republika Srpska Krajina who are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the names mentioned in the Bosnian indictment.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Although it's the same count number, if I remember correctly, but we will check this now.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names mentioned here are those of Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Biljana Plavsic, General Ratko Mladic, and they are not mentioned in the so-called Croatian indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please say the paragraph you're reading from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7, paragraph 7 of the so-called Bosnian indictment. There are four names here that were not mentioned before as participants in the so-called joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What are these names, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Biljana Plavsic, and General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the leadership of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have talked about the participants of the JCE in the list you mentioned apart from these four names. Please be kind enough to tell us about these names and what your attitude was to this. Let's start with Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time in my life that I met Radovan Karadzic was sometime in the second half of March 1991. I was heading a delegation of the Serb Radical Party, and we arrived in Pale. We spoke about general political matters, about the situation in all Serb lands, and Radovan Karadzic was especially interested in our view of the situation in Serbia after the well-known 9th of March events. This was something caused by the pro-Western political parties. Our next meeting was on the 6th of May, 1992, when I arrived again in Republika Srpska. I was near Novak's cave in Romanija, where there was a big rally held, and I had an appointment. A TV broadcast had been scheduled on TV Sarajevo, and this was again in 1991. There were demonstrations by some Muslim political factors against my appearance on the show, and the show was cancelled. Aleksandar Tijanic and Mirjana Bobic Mojsilovic, who were hosts of the TV show, were almost lynched. I visited my sister in Grbavica in Sarajevo, I visited my father's grave in an area populated mainly by Muslims, and I did all this without any incident although many people saw me. However, they did attack the TV show hosts who had arrived from Belgrade to do a show on television Sarajevo. I had friendly relations with Radovan Karadzic, but he was always much more friendly with Zoran Djindjic and Vojislav Kostunica than he was with me, because Radovan Karadzic was jealous of our political party. We had our radical political party in Serbia, and he didn't want somebody there to compete with him in Republika Srpska, especially when it came to patriotism. He was in a coalition with the Serbian Renewal Movement of Vuk Draskovic, and when the Serb deputies were being -- were leaving the Assembly because the Muslims and the Croats wanted to outvote the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, can I ask you, what do you understand so incensed the Muslim political factors that they demonstrated against the television broadcast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was well known all over the former Yugoslavia as a leading Serb nationalist. Certain Muslim factors were provoked by the fact that in public and categorically I asserted that there was no Muslim nation, that this was an artificial nation constructed by the communists and that these were in fact Serbs of the Islamic religion whose origins were Serbian, who spoke the Serb language, and who during the Turkish occupation converted to Islam in order to preserve their social status or to rise on the social ladder. And that was what incensed some Muslim political readers. As far as I can recall, they were not from the government, they were opposition politicians. Their leader, Muhamed Filipovic, spoke at this protest rally, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened, Mr. Seselj? What was the relations -- what were the relations like between the Serb deputies in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina in view of their party membership when there was outvoting and that night session without the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the parliamentary elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a firm coalition was established between the Serb Democratic Party of Radovan Karadzic and the Serb Renewal Movement of Vuk Draskovic who had several deputies there. Not many; three, four, five at the most. But this was significant. All the Serb parties were in solidarity with each other. These two parties left the session of the -- of the Assembly and established an Assembly of the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After this, they were also joined by deputies from the reform forces, a movement led by Ante Markovic, and Dragan Kalinic was their leader in the Assembly. Dragan Kalinic also joined the Assembly of the Serb people and I don't know how much time elapsed before he became a member of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you are talking about Radovan Karadzic now, tell me, what was your cooperation about, and can it be linked in any way to Mr. Nice's allegations?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our positions were patriotic in principle. Mr. Karadzic was also a Serb nationalist, and he was your ideological opponent because he was an anti-communist, an anti-leftist. I can't say that your party was a communist one later on, but it was a leftist party so you couldn't have been on the same wavelength ideologically. Both the Serb Radical Party and Radovan Karadzic's Serb Democratic Party advocated the rehabilitation of the Serb Chetnik movement. Your Socialist Party was always categorically against the rehabilitation of the Serb Chetnik movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you to what extent your relations with Radovan Karadzic can support allegations about some kind of, let's put it mildly, antagonistic standpoint toward Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic did not have an antagonistic attitude to Muslims and Croats. First of all, Radovan Karadzic warned the Muslims in time. He told them not to move towards secession because it might lead to a bloody conflict in which the Muslims would suffer. I can't quote him verbatim, but that's the gist of what he said in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina before independence was declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify, then. Karadzic, according to your knowledge and from all your relations with him, never had a negative attitude toward Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in principle. Later on, he had intensive cooperation with the Croats throughout the war. There was a high degree of cooperation between him and Boban, who was the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, as it was called. Later on it became the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, if I remember rightly. And on more than one occasion he saved the Croats. The army of Republika Srpska, for example, saved the Croats from Vares when there was fierce fighting there between the Muslims and Croats and the Croatian civilians were encircled. He saved about 10.000 people. In Herzegovina, in Kiseljak, in Central Bosnia and so on, they cooperated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Serbs did not fight against the Croats in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the year 1991. Before the beginning of the real war in Bosnia and Herzegovina when the Croatian paramilitary forces took Western Herzegovina and then there was a showdown between these paramilitary forces and the JNA on the -- in the so-called Mostar theatre, later on there were never any real conflicts with the Croats until 1995. In 1995, there were -- there was fighting after the bombing of Republika Srpska, because then the Croatian army together with the Muslim army attacked on all fronts, and with the help of Western fighter planes they took a large part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with your relationship with Radovan Karadzic, can you say anything that might indicate that either Radovan or you had a negative attitude towards Muslims? Let's put the Croats aside because there was no conflict with them.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a civil war going on between the Orthodox Serbs and the Muslims. We were on the side of the Orthodox Serbs. We took sides in that war. He was leading Republika Srpska, I was leading a nationalist Serb party. In the war, of course we were supporting our own side. We were rooting for our own side. We wanted our own side to win, but we never despised the Muslims. There was no condescension, there was no hatred. We very often pointed out the Muslims had been misused in this war against the Serbs and that they were suffering fighting for foreign interests, not their own.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over the weekend I found some documents which fit into this set of questions put to Mr. Seselj regarding the activities of Mr. Karadzic from that time. As, unfortunately, I was unable to copy this over the weekend, I only have the version in Serbian and in English, so I will ask Mr. Seselj to read from the text in Serbian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. You will seek our permission first as to whether you can proceed in that way. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Might we know what category of document it is first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, let us know what this is about. What does it pertain to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an order by Radovan Karadzic, issued on the 19th of August, 1992. So the year is 1992. And I will ask Mr. Seselj whether he knows anything about this kind of activity and this kind of effort. It's also been translated into English, and it's signed by Radovan Karadzic because it was sent at the time to international factors as well, who were already in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let the English version be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it in my binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I just found it over the weekend, so I will ask you to look at it. On page 1, it says -- do you see this order is addressed to the Main Staff of the Serbian Republic. That was its name at the time. The Ministry of Interior and all security police centres.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, I don't speak English, so please give me the version in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will give you the version in Serbian. Then I will not have a copy before me, but I will ask you then to read out the most important points, including this ending. But what I've underlined, as it's a brief order, I think you'll find it easy to just read out the main points. My question, Mr. Seselj, is as follows: Are you aware of the activities and efforts by the leadership of Republika Srpska headed by Radovan Karadzic with a view to solving the questions mentioned in this order? Please read it out and they can see the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this document Radovan Karadzic, as president of the Serbian Republic, addresses himself to the General Staff of Republika Srpska, all security service centres, and the Ministry of Interior, and he says: "According to our official act or enactment of the 13th of June, 1992, concerning respect for international laws of war, I reiterate my order." So it's not the first time he's issuing this order. "That all obligations of the international humanitarian law, especially the 3rd and the 4th Geneva Conventions be implemented by all subjects. "2. That instructions must be issued to all the soldiers and all officers of the Ministry of the Interior to respect prisoners, civilians, medical facilities, private and public places, the Red Cross emblem and personnel and entities of the United Nations. "3. That forced transfer of people and other illegal measures against civilian population must be prevented. Any certificates on the sale of property or written statements by refugees whereby they undertake not to return are legally null and void. "4. That measures be immediately taken to improve conditions in all places of detention in the Serbian Republic in accordance with recommendations given by the International Red Cross on the occasion of their visit to these places, pursuant to the previous decision. All prisoners of war who are not in good health, et cetera, and those who are likely not to join the enemy army soon to be unilaterally released. "5. To inform the International Red Cross immediately about all places of detention in the Serbian Republic and to provide the International Red Cross with exact and full lists of names of persons detained in these places. "6. That all members of the army and the police of the Serbian Republic are under obligation to provide every support to the personnel of the ICRC, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, and other humanitarian organisations. Full safety must be provided to these persons as well as access to all places of detention for prisoners of war." A general instruction: "All bodies of the army and the police in their respective zones of responsibility are obliged to carry out full investigation in case of any suspicion or sign of violation of international humanitarian rights." This is -- this bears the number 01-530/92, August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I know you are grateful to Judge Kwon who points out that this is already Defence Exhibit 190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 193, rather.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Mr. Kwon. I know it has been exhibited, and I am presenting it now because I wanted to hear Mr. Seselj's response concerning his knowledge about the efforts of Republika Srpska leadership and especially its president, Radovan Karadzic, to undertake the necessary measures to protect members of the Muslim and Croat ethnic communities and all citizens regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want a short answer. That's the kind of question that can invite a very long answer, but I want a very short answer on that issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I am in a position to impart to you some personal knowledge that I have from talking to Radovan Karadzic personally in June 1996 that is not reflected in this document. I was with a delegation of the Serbian Radical Party, together with my deputy Tomislav Nikolic, Mr. Poplasen, our representative for Republika Srpska, Mirko Blagojevic, and some other close associates of mine. This was a day-long conversation with Radovan Karadzic in Gorane, near Pale. That was year 1996, the month of June. Momcilo Krajisnik, Nikola Koljevic were present. Biljana Plavsic joined us later. I asked, among other things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Does it relate to the question of the observance of international humanitarian --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear you briefly on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked Mr. Radovan Karadzic several questions that had to do with Srebrenica. Mr. Karadzic said in no uncertain terms that Serb forces had not expelled Muslim civilians. He said that Serb forces had offered to Muslim civilians to remain there under full protection. However, the representative of Muslim civilians insisted that they should leave. An agreement was then signed about voluntary departure of Muslim civilians. It was signed by the Muslim representative, on the Serb side it was signed by Deronjic, and it was co-signed by the major of the Dutch battalion. He showed me this document. I don't have a copy right now, but this document must exist in the archives of Republika Srpska. He showed me this document signed by the Muslim representative, by Deronjic, and by the Dutch major. It said that Muslims would leave of their own accord with transport provided by Serb forces. I next asked him about the treatment of prisoners of war. He said that nobody from the political or military top leadership gave any order to execute prisoners. He said that an execution occurred of 1.000 prisoners that they could not control. He said an investigation was under way and there is indication of involvement by foreign intelligence services. I asked him, "What about a larger number, several thousand, maybe even 8.000?" He said, "We have a figure of 1.000. However, many Muslims were killed while trying to break through Serb encirclement and there were armed Muslims who were killed in fighting. Some Muslims were killed in their internal clashes that occurred when they started arguing about whether to surrender or not." He said that the total figure of all missing Muslims included, according to some people, some Muslims who went missing before Srebrenica fell into Serb hands. And I personally established that on the monument to Muslims killed in Srebrenica there are names of some Muslims who -- who were expelled from Montenegro in 1992 by Mile Djukanovic and they were later executed by Deronjic. According to Radovan Karadzic, this figure was 1.200. However, all the Muslims ever killed in that area or ever gone missing in that area were put together to arrive at that very large figure in order to put the blame on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Seselj, in this order that you just quoted, it says that forcible transfer and other unlawful measures against civilian population should be prevented, and any certificates on the sale of property or statements to the effect that refugees would not return are null and void. Do you know what kind of measures were taken by the leadership and by Radovan Karadzic to protect the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. There was a movement of Muslims accompanied by the signing of various contracts on the sale of property to Serbs. Radovan Karadzic intervened to prevent this on the premise that it was not an expression of their free will but a result of pressure. And there were problems on the ground. There were many spontaneous, unlawful activities on all the three sides. That's simply something that was brought on by the civil war and could not be controlled. Radovan Karadzic kept trying, through this and similar orders, to prevent this kind of thing as much as possible. Sometimes various local governments would take certain decisions of their own accord, arbitrarily. I already mentioned the example of Deronjic in Bratunac. There were similar cases in other areas, Republika Srpska. Republika Srpska authorities frequently intervened to prevent this kind of thing, and they were not always successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While we are still on this issue, namely your knowledge about the measures taken by Radovan Karadzic, I would kindly ask you to look at one letter that he sent - I have the English version, Mr. Robinson - that he sent on the 8th of September, 1992, to Mrs. Ogata in UNHCR, and to the president of the ICRC in Geneva. It's a three-page letter, but I will not go through the entire letter with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic, of which you are unaware?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a document that I found this weekend, Mr. Robinson. I have it in English, the way it was sent to Mrs. Ogata and Mr. Sommaruga, but I have the Serbian version as well, signed by Radovan Karadzic, to put before the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the English version be placed on the ELMO. It does sound familiar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please put the English version on the ELMO, and I will mark it for you. I will highlight the portions I want to look at. And please give the Serbian version to Mr. Seselj. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Seselj, look at the highlighted quotation on the last page and read it. My question relates to alleged forcible deportation that was qualified as ethnic cleansing of Muslims or non-Serb civilians. Would you please read the passage that I highlighted on the last page, which also bears the signature of Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, Radovan Karadzic writes the following: "On the 30th of December [as interpreted] and the 1st of October, 1992, in Geneva, authorised representatives of all the three parties to the conflict in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina met again and adopted a recommendation on The Tragic Situation Of Civilians In Bosnia And Herzegovina. This recommendation was addressed to the international conference on the former Yugoslavia. Item 1 of the Recommendation reads as follows: Civilians who wish to do so should be allowed to leave temporarily the territory controlled by one of the parties in order to go to the territory controlled by another party." Item 3 of the same Recommendation reads as follows: "Civilians should be allowed to leave in an organised fashion under international supervision, and if necessary, protection. Their safety shall be guaranteed by each party in the territory that it controls."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, is this a quotation from an agreement reached in Geneva between the three parties involved in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the effect that civilians should be enabled to freely move from territories held by one party to territories controlled by another party?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an agreement between Serbs and Croats, with foreign mediation. The situation, I must say, was very chaotic on the ground. There was spontaneous movements of civilians as well as expulsions, but in this case the greatest problem were cases where civilians were forced to remain in the territory held by a party to which they were not affiliated. For instance, Muslim authorities prevented Serbs who wanted to leave Sarajevo from leaving for a long time, and police -- Muslim police and paramilitary organisations killed over 4.000 Serb civilians in Kazani and some other places. There are cemeteries that testify to that. Also, they forced civilians to dig trenches in very dangerous places. The purpose of this document is to protect civilians and to respect their freely expressed wish to leave the territory controlled by a party which is their enemy and to move to the territory held by another party which they considered to be theirs. This was followed by the organisation -- organised movement of Serb civilians from Sarajevo protected by international forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I clarify one thing with you. The part that you read talks about temporary movement. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was believed that after cessation of hostilities, after the war ended, that every civilian would be able to return to their home, to where they lived before. However, for the duration of hostilities, civilians were deemed to be unsafe in the territory controlled by a hostile party, and they had many reasons to fear, because they suffered a lot from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You explained it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it mentioned that this agreement on the free movement of civilians was reached by all three parties in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the main purpose was to provide maximum protection of civilians from persecutions, killing, all sorts of suffering, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we then talk about forced deportations of civilians performed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're tiring me with these leading questions which you well know to be impermissible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We shall move on to the next person listed together with you in paragraph 7 of the Bosnian indictment. You have already said a couple of words about the activities of Radovan Karadzic. The next person listed here is Momcilo Krajisnik. What do you know about his activities, and what were your relations with him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My relations with Momcilo Krajisnik were always better than my relations with Radovan Karadzic. We were closer. They were more friendly. There was more trust between us. Karadzic always preferred the company of Djindjic and Kostunica to mine, whereas Krajisnik had more sympathy for me and the Radical Party. However, at a certain point there occurred a dispute between us.
