At some rallies in Republika Srpska, I attacked the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska, Momcilo Mandic, as a criminal, whereas he defended him and tried to tell me that I should not attack him. This Momcilo Mandic appeared in the trial testifying against Krajisnik, proving that he is a criminal after all. In 1996, Krajisnik wrote a letter of support to the Serb Radical Party at the elections in Serbia, whereas Radovan Karadzic and Biljana Plavsic were still in a firm alliance that supported the pro-Western coalition called Zajedno, meaning together. Djindjic, Draskovic, Kostunica and other people were in that party. So that was a clear difference between the political orientation of Krajisnik on the one hand and Plavsic and Karadzic on the other hand. I have a good opinion of Krajisnik as a person and our relations are still friendly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the next person on this list is Biljana Plavsic. What were your relations with Biljana Plavsic, and what can you tell us about her activities from that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never friendly with Biljana Plavsic. We met several times. At first those were courtesy talks, and then we moved into open hostility. I attacked her publicly in 1993, when in an interview to a Belgrade magazine called Nin she stated that it would not be a problem even if 5 million Serbs get killed in that war if only that would secure the survival and freedom of the remaining 5 million Serbs. After that, I stopped all communication with her. As for Biljana Plavsic, at this meeting with Radovan Karadzic and his closest associates that I had in June 1996, I spent an entire day trying to persuade Radovan Karadzic not to nominate Biljana Plavsic for president of Republika Srpska. I stated several arguments; that she is an unstable personality, that she isn't normal, that she doesn't deserve trust, that people who have no children should not occupy such positions because such people are inclined to behave as if --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... characteristic in the observations this witness gives about various named individuals. He's now turning to somebody who has appeared before the Tribunal and whose case has been disposed of. It's not for me in any way to seek to defend her or anybody else, but I wonder if these personal observations, particularly some of the more recent ones, are appropriate and whether they should be encouraged or disallowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there's a delicate balance, Mr. Nice. I believe Mr. Milosevic is trying to elicit evidence to counter the allegation of a joint criminal enterprise, and so the witness is being invited to give evidence that distances himself from these persons, and to the extent that he can show that these are persons who had characteristics that he didn't like or with whom he was not in favour, it may be marginally relevant. But, Mr. Seselj, I would invite you to -- to tone down your comments of a personal nature on these persons mentioned in paragraph 7, because the point, if you have one, can be made -- can be made without those personal remarks. Yes, next question, Mr. Milosevic. Next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please say something very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. I think it's important. Mr. Robinson, I'm not saying what I think of Biljana Plavsic today. I am testifying to what I was telling Radovan Karadzic about Biljana Plavsic in June 1996, before she was nominated for president of the republic. Please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It shows your state of mind, I suppose. But is it really relevant to your state of mind, Mr. Milosevic? That's the issue, because it is you who are on trial, not Mr. Seselj, in these proceedings at any rate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I bear in mind, Mr. Robinson, that paragraph 7 to which Mr. Seselj speaks, this paragraph 7 enumerates some people as members of the joint criminal enterprise, and his testimony is about the relations he had with each of them, and this shows to what extent there were any relationships, let alone within a joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The evidence that goes to show whether Mr. Seselj had or did not have some kind of a relationship, criminal as it may be, with these persons is not necessarily evidence that supports your case that you were not a member of this joint criminal enterprise, because Mr. Seselj is not your alter-ego. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj is of course not my alter ego, but Mr. Seselj knows very well what the relationships were in that time and he can tell us whether such an enterprise existed at all and what kind of relationships the people enumerated in the paragraph had at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic, proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one other comment: You should never lose sight of the fact that you can readily be in a criminal enterprise with a large number of people who never meet each other. The question is your links with them, the essential question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I hope that Mr. Seselj has very -- has fully explained the commitment and efforts made by me personally and the leadership of the Republic of Yugoslavia to accept or to have accepted the peace plans and the attitude to these plans by the people mentioned here. And we can see from his testimony that there were strongly opposed opinions, clashing opinions on the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and these peace initiatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, do you believe that you have sufficiently explained this relationship and the position of Biljana Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer that. Don't answer that. Mr. Milosevic knows very well that he can't put a question like that. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the role of Mrs. Plavsic in the political life of Republika Srpska during the war and after the war, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: She held very extremist positions during the war, insufferably Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. extremist, even for me, and they bothered even me as a declared Serb nationalist. She brought Arkan and his Serb Volunteer Guard to Bijeljina, and she continued to visit him after their activities in Bijeljina and the surrounding area. Sometime in early 1993, Biljana Plavsic sent a letter to Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan, Mirko Jovic, and me, with a demand to send her volunteers. I ignored that letter, but I suppose a copy exists in her archives. And what the other two replied, I don't know. But what matters here are the motives of Radovan Karadzic that drove him to nominate her for president of the republic. He believed her to be more extreme than himself in every way. He thought that the Western protagonists who tried to eliminate him at any cost would have an even greater problem with her. She was known to refuse to shake your hand, to refuse all contact with you. In any case, Radovan Karadzic believed that she would continue to occupy her patriotic positions until the end. However, several months after she was elected, Biljana Plavsic changed her political orientation by 180 degrees under the influence of some Western protagonists and changed her policies completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The last person in this paragraph 7 is Mr. Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, before you move to Mladic. You gave one example of Mrs. Plavsic's extremism, her refusal to shake hands with Mr. Milosevic. Can you give me another example? That is, before she changed her position, as you say, 180 degrees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this has to do with glaring facts. Biljana Plavsic made public statements to the media; radio, press, television. It is generally well known that her positions were extreme, very extreme. She was popularly known as the Serbian Empress because of this extremism of hers. And now to remember exactly what her statements were verbatim, I'm not sure I am going to present her exact words, and I don't want my testimony under oath to be unreliable in any way, but there is an enormous number of statements that she made to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, let us deal with General Mladic as briefly as possible. What was your relationship with him, and what do you know about his activities during the war, and what kind of contacts did you have?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never had any real contacts. We had one brief telephone conversation while General Mladic was in the Knin Corps with the rank of colonel, in November 1991. This was just a courtesy telephone conversation. We never actually met then. I only met his commander, General Vukovic, at that time, who secured a helicopter for me to return to Knin to Belgrade via Mostar and Podgorica. I also had two chance meetings with General Mladic in Belgrade in passing, as it were. As a matter of courtesy, we were just introduced. He even wore civilian clothes. So I did not have any communication with him. However, I attacked him publicly several times, even at rallies in Republika Srpska, when he disobeyed the civilian leadership. In 1995, he -- Radovan Karadzic tried to remove him. General Mladic refused to do so. He was supported by generals of the army of Republika Srpska, and there was great unrest in Republika Srpska at the time, and the entire Republika Srpska was in a state of crisis. I then sided with Radovan Karadzic, and after that I really had no contact with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before we leave paragraph 6 of the Croatian indictment, I'm just going to --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're dealing now with the so-called Bosnian indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but we're going to go back to the Croatian indictment. I omitted to ask you about a particular detail. You spoke about Krajina. You spoke about eastern and western Slavonia. There is a reference there to the Dubrovnik Republic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this Dubrovnik Republic, and how did that happen to be on this list of crimes ascribed to me? Can you say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea of a Republic of Dubrovnik was publicly launched by Novak Kilibarda, then president of the People's Party of Montenegro in 1991. Towards the end of the September or beginning of October 1991, I went to visit the Dubrovnik and Herzegovina front. At that time in southern Herzegovina, there was a clash between the JNA and the Croatian paramilitary forces in the area of Dubrovnik. I took a plane to Podgorica and as I was waiting for a vehicle to take me to Trebinje, I visited Novak Kilibarda at the headquarters of the People's Party in Podgorica. Milorad Albijenic [phoen] was with me, a well-known Serb political activist from Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you because I should have asked Mr. Milosevic to reformulate the question. The question is too general, "Do you know anything about this Dubrovnik Republic?" What is it specifically that you wish to ask the witness? Because a question like that just invites a long, general, meandering answer, which is what we were getting. So focus the witness on a specific issue in relation to the concept, the idea of a Dubrovnik Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, since you know the entire political situation from that time very well, this idea of a Dubrovnik Republic from that time - I'm not talking about the historical aspect or any other aspect now - does it have anything to do with Serbia, the leadership of Serbia, and me personally?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not with you personally, not with the leadership of Serbia, but when Novak Kilibarda launched this idea, we from the Serb Radical Party supported the idea. There was a group of Serb Catholics from Dubrovnik and Cavtat there too. They set up a committee for establishing a Dubrovnik Republic and Nova Kilibarda supported them. The Serb Radical Party in that year, 1991, did not set up its own party organisation in Montenegro because we supported the People's Party of Novak Kilibarda. It was only in May 1992 when, at the suggestion of the American ambassador in Belgrade Kilibarda decided to boycott federal elections in Montenegro, we, the Serb Radicals, in great haste organised our own party branch in Montenegro and became part of the elections, and that is when we severed all contacts with Kilibarda and his party in 1991. Our relationship was a cordial one and we supported his initiative to renew the Republic of Dubrovnik which had had a tradition many centuries long, because it was the Serb Catholics who had actually established the Republic of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is said here that you launched this idea and advocated it in the area of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political milieu of only one political party in Montenegro, the People's Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So at that time the People's Party was not in power in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. It was an opposition party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: An opposition party to the DPS or, rather, the Democratic Party of Socialists of Momir Bulatovic in which Mile Djukanovic was Prime Minister and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Momir Bulatovic, Mile Djukanovic, did they have anything to do with this idea of the Dubrovnik Republic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard any one of the two of them advocating the Dubrovnik Republic. I never heard anyone else do that except for Novak Kilibarda, and we, the Serb Radicals, supported him in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 26 now, which is rather long. It's in the Croatian part. It's on page 5. It has subparagraphs (a) through (l). In connection with that, I'm going to put a few questions to you. What it says here is the following. We're looking at paragraph 26 and the ways are listed in which allegedly the joint criminal enterprise was carried out, and you took part in it too, purportedly. So how was it carried out? It says: "Slobodan Milosevic, acting alone and in concert with other members of the joint criminal enterprise -" and we've just commented upon all of them now, all of those that are listed - "participated in the joint criminal enterprise in the following ways ..." And then in subparagraph (a), it says: "Provided direction and assistance to the political leadership of the SAO SBWS, the SAO Western Slavonia, SAO Krajina and RSK on the take-over of these areas and the subsequent forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population." Mr. Seselj, a few moments ago you mentioned who was in power in those areas. You mentioned Martic and Babic, Dokmanovic, Sergej Veselinovic, then Zdravko Zecevic. So an entire series of Serbs were in power in these municipalities. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those Serbs came to power through elections, local elections, in the territory of the Croatian federal unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But if somebody was already in power, could he take power?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but could expand his own authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Was it someone from Serbia who appointed these people to govern in Croatia or were they already in power in Croatia when the Serbs in Croatia were imperiled by what the Croatian regime was doing?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of these people were already in power. For example, Slavko Dokmanovic was already the mayor of Vukovar before the armed hostilities started in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Babic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Babic was president of the Knin municipality. Every one of them was either head of a municipality or head of a police in a municipality, so they were already officials of the local government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when local tensions and conflicts started?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can it be said, then, that it was anyone that assisted them in taking over power?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if I formed the view that you are being provocative in asking these leading questions time and again, I will adopt a certain measure. Reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this is one of the key questions here, because it says here, "assisted people in the take-over of these areas."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have stopped you because that is not the issue. The issue is the way the question was put, "Can it be said, then, that it was anyone that assisted them in taking over power?" The witness is to give his evidence unaided.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, when did these people come to power in these municipalities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after these elections that were held in the federal unit of Croatia. As far as I remember, it was the end of April, beginning of May 1990, if my memory serves me correctly. That is to say before the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hostilities broke out, they were already in power in all these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, the second part of subparagraph (a) says that they were given assistance in the subsequent forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population. Did they forcibly remove the Croat and other non-Serb population, as is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I remember a particular case, the village of Kijevo in the municipality of Knin. When I was there at the end of 1991, I had my own personal pistol on me. We went through those -- through that village -- to that village through Serb village -- or, rather, we had to go through the village of Kijevo in order to get to other Serbian villages. Matic's police told us to give the policemen our own weapons before entering the village so that some local policemen would not stop us there and find that we had weapons on our persons. All of that shows that Matic's police acted very delicately, trying to avoid any kind of incident. We all handed over our weapons, we peacefully went through this purely Croat village of Kijevo and visited all the other Serb-populated villages. However, when the hostilities broke out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, just remind me, I'm trying to remember, what post did you occupy at that time? This is 1991 -- 1991, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I was president of an opposition party, the Serb Radical Party, and I was the only MP of my party in the Assembly of Serbia, the one and only one. At that time we were still a small political party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And exactly how did you acquire information and knowledge about these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was there. I was in Knin. I'm telling you about my own experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We established when they came to power, and we established how they came to power, and we established when.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict in the elections in 1990. And when the HDZ came to power, did the new government try to disempower the Serbs in the Krajina at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Through the break-ins of their own specialists in police stations that were commanded by Serbs and where most policemen were ethnic Serbs. They seized their weapons and their warehouses. That was a sufficient signal for the Serbs that a great evil was in the making for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the local population?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were demonstrations. Civilians opposed Croatian specialists, and there were conflicts. There was a conflict in Pakrac sometime in the beginning of March 1991. Then there was the conflict in Plitvice and in many other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, it is said about you, in addition to what we've already said, that you openly espoused the concept of a Greater Serbia, but let's leave that aside, but it also says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a reference, and it is too fast anyway, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking for a reference. Were you then referring to a particular paragraph in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 22. Paragraph 22, and it says, in addition to what we've already elaborated, that is to say Greater Serbia, it says: "... by violence and other unlawful means, and actively participated in war propaganda and spreading inter-ethnic hatred."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So going back to that time, did you advocate violence and other unlawful means and actively participate in war propaganda and spreading inter-ethnic hatred? In the context of these events, not generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There has to be a clear distinction between two matters, that is the concept of a Greater Serbia and the civil war that took place. The concept of a Greater Serbia cannot be realised without us convincing previously Serb Catholics and Serb Muslims that we are one and the same people. We had to make every effort there to oppose the 100-year-long policy of the Vatican and the 40-year-old policy of the Communist Party. They invented the Croatian people and the Muslim people within the Serb ethnic being. And secondly, the war that took place was not caused by the Serbs. The war was caused by those who wanted to break up Yugoslavia. I supported armed efforts made by the Yugoslav People's Army to defeat paramilitary formations of Tudjman's regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what is on the transcript. "They invented the Croatian people and the Muslim people within this Serb ethnic being."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation is incorrect. This is about the Croatian nation and the Muslim nation. To explain this to you, let me remind you of the example of France. The ethnic substrate there has created a unified nation. In our parts, the process went in the opposite direction. On the Serbian ethnic substrate, based on religious differences, three nations were formed and the Serbs were reduced to just the Orthodox Serbs, and they were separated from the Catholic Serbs and the Muslim Serbs. I hope this is clearer to you. This is unprecedented anywhere in the whole world. Everywhere else, the Muslims are simply a religion. Nowhere are they a separate nation. I hope that is clearer to you now. Of course, everyone who comes in from the outside finds this very odd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You haven't answered a part of my question, the part where it says that acting as part of this alleged joint criminal enterprise you actively participated in war propaganda and spreading inter-ethnic hatred, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, the question arises of what kind of war propaganda this was. Was it institutionalised war propaganda behind which there is a state institution and I participated in that? Well, if that's what's alleged, my answer is a categorical no. However, I do admit that many of my statements as an individual politician and as the president of the Serb Radical Party appeared to many to resemble warmongering. This may have been the case, but it had nothing to do with some kind of organised institutionalised propaganda. Secondly, the spreading of inter-ethnic hatred is a very broad concept. Someone could say that I'm spreading inter-ethnic hatred when I say that the Muslims are not a separate nation. I am basing my statements, however, on scientific facts, so I feel it is not spreading inter-ethnic hatred while other people feel it is because I am attacking the fundamental -- the foundation of that nation. In the case of the Croats, I attacked only the Croatian Ustasha without any limitations. But as for most Croats, I attempted to prove that they are actually Serbs, because what happened was that when the Serb nation was split up, the new Croatian nation was composed of three segments, three different ethnic substrates; Original Croats who speak the Chakavian language, original Slovenes who speak the Kajkavian language and they live in the so-called Croatian Zagorje region, and the original Serb Catholics who speak the Shtokavian language, and that is the Serbian language. So I base everything I say on scientific arguments. My speeches may have been fiery, they're always fiery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you spread hatred in that way?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not spread hatred. I spread love. I was trying to convince people who had fallen away from the Serb nation that they were actually Serbs and that we had to renew brotherhood and unity between Serbs of the Orthodox, Croat, and Muslim religions and that we had to have a joint state.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to the then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Look at the transcript, Mr. Milosevic. The interpreters are asking for a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is becoming unbearable. And I'm not satisfied that you are trying hard enough, Mr. Milosevic, and Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think everything has been interpreted now, so I will repeat my question and I will speak as slowly as possible. Mr. Seselj -- or, rather, slowly enough for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of this organising on the territory of the Krajina, Eastern Slavonia, Western Slavonia, Knin, and so on, according to the then regulations beginning with the constitution, was it permissible for municipalities to associate?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the constitutions of the former Yugoslavia permitted the association of municipalities. The only discrepancy was this independent formation of autonomous provinces, but this was actually a response to the previous violations of the constitution by the authorities in Croatia and later Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to the then regulation that you are familiar with, what was the basis and the purpose of the association of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipalities could associate to form regional communities in order to pursue various interests which could be of an economic nature, a social nature, a political nature. So these were various interests, but this was usually done by neighbouring municipalities, and by associating they could achieve certain results easier, and they could save their resources in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me now, the leaderships we have just mentioned in this paragraph that we have quoted, did they forcibly remove the non-Serb population, and did I assist them in that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no organised forcible removal of the Croatian and other non-Serb population. There was a certain spontaneous movement of the population. There may have been individual inter-ethnic incidents, but many Croatian officials invited the Croatian population --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or, rather, many Serb politicians, interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- invited them to stay, promising them protection and so on and so forth, and this was reported in the media. But there was another phenomenon: The Croatian population began to arm themselves illegally in these municipalities. They were armed by Tudjman's government. I can give you a specific example. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. A few days ago I testified about my participation in the peaceful demonstration, the march on Plitvice. On that day when we had the march to Plitvice and -- well, it may be exaggerated to call them clashes with JNA units, but we did meet opposition from the JNA, and I returned to Knin. On that day, Martic's police, carrying out a routine check of some Croat houses of Croats living in Knin, and they found new automatic rifles produced in Hungary concealed in shipments of flour, in sacks of flour. One of these automatic rifles of Hungarian origin Milan Martic gave to me. He as the chief of police gave it to me as a sign of gratitude for contributing to making this march a success, making it peaceful while achieving its goals. I had this rifle for some time. It's a Kalashnikov, and it's of lesser quality than our rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, now, as we are now speaking of aid, what was the reason for providing aid to the Krajina Serbs by the Republic of Serbia, and what did this aid consist in?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was political assistance and material assistance. When I say material, I refer to food and money. Political support was provided because Serbia wanted the Serbs living across the Danube to be protected in their vital and existential rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Subparagraph (b) of this paragraph reads as follows: Provided all kinds of assistance to "regular and irregular military forces necessary for the take-over of these areas and the subsequent forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia did not provide any kind of support to any irregular military forces, because with the few rare exceptions I have mentioned referring to the Serb Volunteer Guard, the White Eagles, and so on and so forth, it was exclusively the regular military forces operating there; the JNA, the local police, and the Territorial Defence under the control of the JNA. Serbia could support only the JNA, as it was obliged to do under the still valid Yugoslav constitution of the time. Secondly, the JNA, which was the only regular armed force operating on the ground there, did not participate in any forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population. Yes, there were individual incidents, but this was never the goal of the JNA and never were orders issued by the higher commands of the JNA to act in this way, or at least, I never heard of any such orders. And we have seen what the structure of the top leadership of the JNA was and how many Croats, Muslims, Slovenes, and others were there. So it was not possible for the JNA to issue an order to have the Croatian population expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm pausing to wait for the end of the interpretation before I put my question to you, Mr. Seselj. You have explained what the regular forces were. Which were the irregular formations in the area?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The irregular formations were those of the so-called National Guard Corps of Croatia, established by Franjo Tudjman. They were colloquial called the Zengas. This was the main paramilitary formation. The Croats had some other spontaneous groups or those under the control of the paramilitary. There was the Glavas -- there were the Glavas units, they were openly Ustasha; then there were the formations of the Croatian Party of Rights, led by Dobroslav Paraga. I cannot remember the names of all these groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'm referring now only to your own experience and your personal knowledge. Were the Krajina Serbs the ones who were doing the attacking or were they the ones who came under attack?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were always under attack. The regime of Franjo Tudjman wanted to return the territory on which they had been living for centuries under his control and the Krajina Serbs opposed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We will not go into expert opinions, but viewed legally, were they justified in their demands?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legally, their efforts were in line with the provisions of the constitution and the legislation. This was done with a view to preserving Yugoslavia. Tudjman's separatist moves were absolutely counter-constitutional. The JNA was acting in accordance with the constitution, and those fighting them on the territory of the Croatian federal unit were violating the constitution, and they were subject to criminal prosecution, because there was a crime of armed rebellion. And the JNA even tried some cases but didn't manage to complete the trials. You may remember the arrest of General Martin Spegelj and the attempts to have him court-martialed in Zagreb, the arrests of some other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, let us now deal very specifically with this question. To whom in the Krajina did the Republic of Serbia provide material and other support, and why?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia provided financial and material assistance only to the legal leadership of the Republic of Srpska Krajina to help them survive, because the Croats were already receiving a lot of assistance from the Western powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will now quote subparagraph (c) of this same paragraph, which reads: "Directed organs of the government of the Republic of Serbia to create armed forces separate from the federal armed forces to --" this is what it says in this text here. I hope you have it before you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "... armed forces -" the Republic of Serbia - "in order to engage in combat activities outside the Republic of Serbia, in particular in the said areas in Croatia and the subsequent forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia never had its armed forces. On the territory of Serbia, there was the Territorial Defence. It was subordinated to the JNA and had no independent role. All those from Serbia who participated in armed activities on the territory of the Croatian federal units were in the JNA. There were also volunteers. In Serbia, they were professional policemen. They wanted to be volunteers in the Republic of Srpska Krajina in any of these autonomous provinces. They would then ask for permission from their higher organs and go there as volunteers while their professional rights from their employment were protected, as were the professional rights of the mobilised reservists of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have answered this question indirectly, but I have to spell it out for you: Did the Republic of Serbia ever form any armed forces apart from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Never did the Republic of Serbia form any armed forces separate from the federal forces, although there were some such initiatives from the opposition parties. In the summer of 1991, the Serb Renewal Movement and another party intensively advocated the formation of a Serbian army. I had a political debate on television with Zoran Djindjic, and we clashed about this point precisely because he was advocating the formation of a Serbian army. I opposed this, and I won in this debate. I supported the JNA as the only regular armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, was there ever a plan in Serbia to form armed forces separate from the Yugoslav armed forces?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government never had any such plan. As I said, it was individuals and opposition political parties who advocated such ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In subparagraph (d) of this same paragraph, it says: "Participated in the formation, financing, supply, support and direction of special forces of the Republic of Serbia Ministry of Internal Affairs. These special forces were created and supported to assist in the execution of the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise through the commission of crimes which are in violation ..." and so on. My question is: What do you know about the special forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs? Where and why were they formed? Who did they -- were they composed of, and so on?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, there was only one special unit of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, the so-called special anti-terrorist unit established in the early 1980s. It was needed because of the events in Kosovo and Metohija. At that time, all federal units started establishing their special anti-terrorist units, and all of these units were involved in suppressing the Albanian separatist insurgency in Kosovo and Metohija from Slovenia, Macedonia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, et cetera, and the Serb special anti-terrorist unit was formed at the same time. To the best of my knowledge, this special anti-terrorist unit was never engaged as such in the wars on the territory of Croatia or Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was only after 1996 that another special unit was set up of the state security department. It was called Special Operations Unit, and they were popularly known as Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that unit, JSO, Special Operations Unit, was established in 1996.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it include some individuals who had some experience in armed conflicts in various areas of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was precisely the idea, to gather in that unit fighters who were tested and tried, the best fighters, to concentrate them in that unit which had about 150 members, because it was believed that such a unit would be needed in the future trials that awaited our country. Some former members of Arkan's Volunteers Guard were included in that unit, as well as some members of -- some former members of Martic's police. I know for a fact that some volunteers of the Serb Radical Party received an offer to become members of that unit, and many of them told me about it, saying at the same time they would reject the offer because at the time the Serb Radical Party was fiercely opposing your regime led by your party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If, because some members of the JSO fought in Krajina and Bosnia and Herzegovina before the JSO itself was established, can it be concluded then that the JSO as such was involved in the wars? Because by the same token we could say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. That's not to be answered. And by this time, Mr. Seselj, you should know, you should be able to recognise the impermissible questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I submit to your will, Mr. Robinson, from day one, even when I'm not very happy to do so, but I always abide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you said this unit for special operations was set up in 1996. Do you have any explanation why the engagement of that unit outside of Serbia is mentioned even before it was formed?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that confusion is due to the use of the term "Red Berets," because various units that took part in these wars called themselves Red Berets. Sometimes the soldiers who had completed the training course in the training centre of Captain Dragan were called Red Berets. Some units Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wore red berets as part of their uniform and the people commonly called them Red Berets. I saw two judgements of this Tribunal, against Blagojevic and against Dragan Jokic, and I read that the VRS had a reconnaissance squad called Red Berets. You can find that in one of your judgements, Mr. Robinson. So various organisations, various groups were referred to as Red Berets. This unit of the state security service became known among people and among its own members as Red Berets. It was their popular name. I think that's what's creating the confusion. However, all of those who had previous war experience were proud of it, and they believed they were fighting for Serb national interests, and they did not see any difference between their previous engagements in other units and their new role in the Special Operations Unit, because we are and we will remain one people, no matter how hard Western powers may try to divide us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will now quote to you a sentence that is unclear to me but maybe you will understand. It's subparagraph (e) of the same paragraph 26: "Participated in providing financial, logistical and political support and direction --" Let me check. Yes: "... providing financial, logistical and political support and direction to Serbian irregular forces and paramilitaries. Such support was given in furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise through the commission of crimes which are in violation ..." et cetera, et cetera. Let me not read the rest. Tell me as briefly as you can, what was the attitude of the authorities in Serbia to paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian authorities were emphatically against paramilitary formations and tried to suppress them. I remember very well because I was a deputy in the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia at the time. We had a very bad legislation inherited from previous times in that area. Possession of weapons did not used to be a crime. It was a misdemeanour, subject to a fine, and the strictest penalty was confiscation. The Serbian Assembly adopted a special law in 1992, according to which any illegal possession of a weapon was a serious crime, subject to three years' imprisonment and more. Movement was prohibited to all uniformed people who were not members of the JNA. That law was enacted in 1992. Until then, there was no such legal protection, so that members of paramilitary units moved around Serbia wearing uniforms, and illegal possession of weapons was treated until then as a misdemeanour, subject to a very mild penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me apologise in advance because I don't want you to think that I'm asking you the same question over and over again. It is simply that an allegation is reiterated in subparagraph (f), which reads: "Participated in the planning and preparation of the take-over of the SAO SBWS, the SAO Western Slavonia, the SAO Krajina and the Dubrovnik Republic and the subsequent forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population." This is a special subparagraph. You have already given some explanations, but I have to ask you again: Did I participate in the take-over of power in the said areas, and what do you know about this alleged removal of non-Serb population and my role therein?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you could not possibly participate in the take-over of power. We established that. Second, you were not in a position to take part in the command over the JNA, and you could not possibly participate in the removal of the Croat and non-Serb population. I visited those theatres of war, and I saw with my own eyes the things I'm going to tell you about. The population from the area of Dubrovnik was joined together with Croatian paramilitary units that had been fighting the JNA. Take Cavtat, a town south of Dubrovnik. Croat paramilitary formations abandoned Cavtat without a fight. Croat civilians remained there to live. The JNA supplied them with food and other necessities. There was no forcible removal or any kind of removal. It is a rather high concentration of the civilian population, Croat Catholic population, and still the JNA tried to help them. There are many other instances of villages that were treated by the JNA in the same way. The Croatian population was removed only in those areas where Croatian paramilitary units or the Croatian government organised the departure of their own civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Look now at subparagraph (g), which reads: "Exerted effective control or substantial influence over the JNA which participated in the planning, preparation and execution of the forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population from..." all the areas already enumerated; Western Slavonia, Western Srem, Krajina, et cetera. Before I ask you how I exerted that effective control, I have to ask you, did the JNA participate in the planning and execution of the forcible removal?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the JNA did not. Its units and troops were not ordered to do so. However, you could not exert any control over the JNA. Throughout 1991, all the way until the Vance-Owen Plan -- correction, until the Vance Plan was accepted, and this is something that General Kadijevic explained in his book that he published after he left his post, the plan was to remove all the political leaderships from all the federal units; Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, et cetera. It was the army plan. The army wanted to take over power, and General Kadijevic thought the Western powers would approve. However, when he lost that hope, he went to Moscow, seeking Russian support, and the Russian Marshal Jazov told me several years later about his conversations with Veljko Kadijevic. Veljko Kadijevic asked for an intervention by the Russian army, and the Russian Marshal Jazov replied to him that the army of the Soviet Union could not interfere because they are not backed by the appropriate decisions of their leadership. Thus Veljko Kadijevic was planning a military putsch, seeking foreign support for it. And being unable to get it either in the East or in the West, he had to abandon the idea in 1991, at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you said the JNA did not participate in this planning, and I think you have explained already the allegations about me exerting effective control, and you said the JNA did not participate in the forcible removal of population. But tell me, how did the JNA act in crisis situations when there were tensions and conflicts between members of various ethnic communities in the area of the former Yugoslavia, and tell me in particular what was the attitude of the JNA towards civilians? How did they treat members of various ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA tried their best to prevent conflicts, to eliminate conflicts, to act as a buffer zone between conflicting parties. I already mentioned the example of Borovo village when a JNA unit moved in only ten minutes after the conflict started, and it ordered the policemen and -- on both sides to withdraw and to take away their wounded. They had orders from the highest command to treat all the civilians equally, with care, to protect them, to assist them in war zones in every possible way. That was the general position of the JNA, and all the orders that I know of were worded to that effect. The JNA did not make any distinction on ethnic grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope the microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We can move on, Mr. Seselj. Subparagraph (h) --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just tell me which page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 6. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Provided financial, logistical and other support to units --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could interpreters have a reference, an exact reference? It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop. The interpreters are asking for a reference. It's paragraph 26 and subparagraph (h) of the Croatian indictment. And, Mr. Milosevic, there is no point reading it out. You ought to be able to formulate a question that reflects the substance of the paragraph. You're wasting time reading out what is in the indictment. In any event, the witness has it in front of him in his own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something that is repeated many times throughout, Mr. Robinson, and it was written by Mr. Nice and his service. I didn't write it. If I wrote that, I wouldn't have to ask the same question over and over again, but these allegations do repeat themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did I provide financial support to some units to carry out some sort of criminal enterprise and did they perpetrate a criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not assist any units of the Territorial Defence because all those units were under the command of the JNA. Your military support, if any, could only have been support to the JNA, whereas the financial and -- financial and logistical support was extended to the political leaderships of those areas. Second, there were no TO units or government agencies in the Dubrovnik Republic. The Dubrovnik Republic remained an idea, an initiative. No institutions were formed to support it, and this is something that's repeated throughout the Croatian indictment. So the Dubrovnik Republic was an initiative of Novak Kilibarda, and a group of deputies from Cavtat, Serb Catholics from Cavtat and other towns. It remained an initiative. In the area of Dubrovnik it was only the JNA that was active. There were no paramilitary units, there were no units of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: TO units are mentioned in all these areas. Is it the case that TO units and volunteer units assist in the execution of this joint criminal enterprise by forcibly removing one-third of the Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forcible deportation of the Croatian population was nobody's objective. Elements of persecution occurred only in the framework of incidents. However, there was no such systematic conduct either as an idea or in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: (i) says I effectively ordered the passage of laws and regulations relative to the involvement of the JNA, the TO, and Serb volunteer units in Croatia. My question is as follows: Are you aware of the existence of any law or regulation that would suit this description, match this description?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was senseless referring to that in the indictment. There cannot be a single law before it is published in the Official Gazette or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the federal Official Gazette. Laws related to the JNA could only be passed by the Federal Assembly and the Presidency of Yugoslavia could adopt decrees with the force of law in a state of war, imminent state of war, or an emergency, a state of emergency. So it could have nothing to do with you or could you order anyone in the federal parliament or federal Presidency to adopt such general or legal enactments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you note the word "effectively" in paragraph (i), which encompasses the idea that although Mr. Milosevic might not have done so de jure, in effect, nonetheless, there was the passage of these laws. But I understand you to say that no laws at all were passed relating to the involvement of the JNA, the TO, and the Serb volunteer units in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I categorically state that no laws regarding this matter were passed. There was no need to do that because the laws of the former Yugoslavia were quite sufficient. On the basis of the laws and regulations of the former Yugoslavia, the chief of General Staff could take orders to have volunteers engaged within the JNA. As far as I know, there are only such orders. And an order cannot be a legal enactment with the force of law, Mr. Robinson. I hope you will agree with me that that doesn't exist anywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I would tend to agree with you, but let us hear the evidence. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you've got the next subparagraph, (j), where it says that I directed, commanded, controlled or otherwise provided substantial assistance or support to the JNA, the Serb-run TO, staff and volunteer forces deployed in the execution of the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is impossible legally and factually, but there's something else I'm thinking of now, Mr. Milosevic. Your political opponents, including myself, sometimes in the heat of arguments did accuse you of this. It seems that the indictment was written on the basis of our attacks against you, not on the basis of actual facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me put a question to you. It says directed, commanded, controlled, or otherwise provided substantial assistance or support to the JNA, the TO, et cetera. Did I do that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's impossible. Command and control is a purely military function, and it takes place according to the military chain of command, the military hierarchy. There was simply no place for you in that military chain of command. I have already implicitly shown that you could not influence Veljko Kadijevic or Blagoje Adzic. You could talk to them. You could advise them, but it was obvious from all testimonies from the period that they practically did not listen to anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could there please be a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking for a pause between question and answer. You also said in your answer, Mr. Seselj, that it was impossible factually. You said this is impossible legally and factually. Now, comment on why it was a factual impossibility for Mr. Milosevic to exercise control over the JNA. We're not dealing now with the de jure legal situation, the chain of command. As a matter of fact, why was it impossible for him for to exercise such control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Factually, it was impossible because of the structure of the command of the Yugoslav People's Army, due to the fact that the minister of defence was General Veljko Kadijevic, and the chief of General Staff was General Blagoje Adzic. The two of them, together with a group of other generals, constantly planned a coup d'etat, military coup d'etat, to topple Mr. Milosevic, Tudjman, Rupel, Izetbegovic, and God knows who else, and to reunite Yugoslavia, expecting foreign support. They were never followers of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, anything is factually possible if it is to happen outside the law. Whether it can happen depends, does it not, on the personality of the individuals that are involved and the power that is open to them, the power that is exercisable by them as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The memoir of Borisav Jovic, then member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, you can see, Mr. Robinson, that Milosevic and Borisav Jovic constantly expressed their dissatisfaction with the behaviour of Kadijevic and Blagoje Adzic. There was some intolerance there that all of us involved in politics were aware of. I myself knew that there was dislike between Milosevic on the one hand and Blagoje Adzic and Veljko Kadijevic on the other hand. As a matter of fact, when learning of this dislike in 1991, my sympathy was on Mr. Milosevic's side rather than on Kadijevic's and Adzic's side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Seselj, precisely on the basis of your knowledge from that time, what was it that could have created the impression that there was an alliance between the JNA, the Serbian leadership, and the Serbs from the areas in Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only because the position of the Serbian leadership and majority political factors were loyal to the Yugoslav People's Army. They did not want to set up a separate army and they did not want to break up Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me just see whether the interpretation has finished. Yes. Fine. Now, advocating the preservation of Yugoslavia, was that unlawful and was that in contravention of the law?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only lawful and right option from the point of view of the constitution and the legal order. Everything else was against the law. Even I, who was ideologically very disappointed in Yugoslavia, from an ideological point of view I no longer found Yugoslavia acceptable. From a legal and factual point of view, I always behaved loyally because Yugoslavia was the only legal state at the time, and its armed force was the only regular army throughout the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it lawful to advocate the breaking up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was unlawful, and it was also in contravention of provisions of the Federal Criminal Code. All of those who pursued a separatist policy, even without resorting to force, because even that was prohibited, could have been sentenced to many years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Advocating the preservation of Yugoslavia and defending of Yugoslavia, was that the right and obligation of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the basic obligation of the JNA throughout its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Along with the JNA, according to the constitution of Yugoslavia, who made up the armed forces of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armed forces were made up of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence. According to the constitution, those are the two components of the armed forces. Laws further stipulated when the TO would be resubordinated to JNA commands, because the Territorial Defence was established at the level of federal units respectively and the JNA only at the level of all of Yugoslavia. The army districts of the JNA did not correspond to the borders of the federal units. For example, the 6th Army District, with its headquarters in Sarajevo, did encompass almost all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and almost all of Slavonia, which belonged to the federal unit of Croatia otherwise, and in Slovenia there were two army districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Advocating the preservation of Yugoslavia and defending it, was that the task of the Territorial Defence too?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, likewise. Both components of the armed forces were duty-bound to safeguard Yugoslavia from external aggression and from internal subversive factors; a possible armed insurrection or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And advocating the preservation of Yugoslavia, was that the obligation of all other organs of government; federal, republic and municipal, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Federal, republican, provincial, municipal, et cetera, all levels of government, and also all citizens were duty-bound to preserve the territorial integrity, the legal order and the state sovereignty of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Support and assistance to the JNA in carrying out its constitutional duties, is that something illegal?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was your duty. Everything you did as president of the Republic of Serbia, everything that your party did as the ruling party in Serbia, in all the institutions of Serbia in the domain of assisting the Yugoslav People's Army was your constitutional and legal obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Generally speaking, Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to slow down and could Mr. Milosevic be asked to read slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking you to slow down. Mr. Seselj, you do not observe the pause after Mr. Milosevic's questions. You answer immediately. Follow Mr. Milosevic. He is now listening to the interpretation and waiting until the interpretation is finished. You answer immediately --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- because you speak the same language, so there is that natural tendency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to pause. If I sometimes get carried away, I hope you won't hold it against me very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, if particular entities in one state, especially the state organs of that state, advocate the survival of that state and defend it from illegal violent secession, which, as you explained, is a constitutional obligation, can that be considered some kind of conspiracy or a joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. I am beginning to form the view now, Mr. Milosevic, that these questions are provocatively leading, and I'm considering a particular course of action to take. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, did the mentioned forces, and you spoke about these forces, the JNA and the Territorial Defence, commit any crimes in order to carry out a joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Crimes did occur, but in particular incidents where it was impossible to control individuals or groups, some groups. To the best of my knowledge, some crimes were intentionally provoked in order to yield political effects. As proof of that, I say, and this is a fact, that General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, as head of the military security service, happened to be in Western Slavonia at the time of the breakdown of Western Slavonia when there were some crimes committed against civilians, and he also happened to be in Vukovar when the prisoners in Ovcara were executed. That shows that some factor in the military, for political reasons, wanted particularly graphic crimes in order to manipulate them later, for manipulative purposes. I simply have no other explanation for what happened. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you are not accusing General Vasiljevic of taking part in what happened.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do accuse him, because General Vasiljevic, if he knew about these crimes in Western Slavonia and in Ovcara, he did not file criminal reports. He did not take appropriate measures for military courts as the only courts that were in charge, according to the legal order then, to prosecute criminally the perpetrators. That was his elementary duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, let's see what subparagraph (k) says of this paragraph number 26. It says that I directed, commanded, controlled or otherwise provided substantial assistance or support to the police forces within the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, including the DB, whose members assisted in the execution of the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise in the SAO, one SAO, the other SAO, and the Dubrovnik Republic. Now, the question is whether the MUP of Serbia took part in carrying out any activities of that nature in the territories that are mentioned here, that is to say all the territories.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of Serbia did not send a single police unit to these areas. Individually, policemen did sign up as volunteers. Among them, Radovan Stojicic Badza. They went to the theatre of war. Their work obligations or, rather, their professional standing was regulated by law like in the case of all other members of the JNA. All of those who were members of the JNA or were volunteers in the JNA remained employed and got leave of absence. In some companies, they even got paid leave of absence because they'd go away for about a month or a month and a half. That was the usual period that the volunteers spent at the front line. As for the Dubrovnik Republic that is referred to here, there was not a single volunteer there from Serbia, let alone a policeman from Serbia who was on duty there. It was only the JNA that was active in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm trying to remember what was the Prosecution case in relation to paragraph (k). Is it that the form of assistance was wholly confined to the physical presence of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, let me help you because I've been concerned that with all these questions the accused has sought general answers where he's been provided months and months ago, if not years ago, with a scheduled, detailed analysis of how the Prosecution puts its case in the document called the fill-box document which was provided for everyone's assistance but not least his given that he's unrepresented and maybe not skilful advocate. Therefore, one can simply go to that document, which has always been available to him and is indeed searchable in electronic form, and see that under paragraph 26(k) you have I think some -- probably a dozen or maybe more than a dozen separate entries, and I'm probably not able to encapsulate them in a single answer to Your Honour's question, but to give you a few examples of the entries that we find there, we find from one witness volunteers fighting in the Vukovar area, many of whom admitted that they worked for the MUP of the government of Serbia. Second entry is in relation to fires in the vicinity of Bihac airport and a major who was there as well as members of the SDB of Serbia. Third entry relates to fairly detailed evidence from Milan Babic. Fourth entry is Exhibit 352, tab 19. It's all set out there, the various ways in which this particular part of the indictment is said to be supported by the Prosecution. And it's not a single way. It's a number of different ways. You can go through, apart from the evidence of Aleksandar Vasiljevic himself, he was referred to, you can also find, and you'll probably, I think, remember this, evidence from -- it's on page 188 of the document, the employee at the Ministry of Defence of Serbia dealing with Dusanko Vorkapic from Sid of the local Serb Territorial Defence for Vukovar coming to the Ministry of Defence, saying that the sewer system was being used by Croat forces as a shelter from which to attack Serbs, and the minister then consulting with the accused and deciding that Arkan's volunteers were to be given the task of mining and stocking up the corridors. It's a great deal of evidence, and it's all been provided to the accused so that if he has the ability, through this witness, to deal with direct -- in direct evidence to counter or qualify the evidence that's been given, he could have been doing so in these direct. These vague or generalised answers are unlikely to assist in the analysis evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. It's for the accused to determine how to put his questions, but I merely wanted to remind myself of what the Prosecution case was on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really wondering, Mr. Robinson, how I'm supposed to prove that the allegations by these alleged witnesses of Mr. Nice's are incorrect. They can say whatever they like. These are merely lies, and I'm asking Mr. Seselj about the counts in this alleged indictment. If you're asking me to prove that his witnesses are telling falsehoods, well, how can I prove non-existent facts? You keep telling me that the burden of proof is not on me, and yet I have to keep trying to prove that what Mr. Nice is saying is not true. It's up to him to prove that it is true. So I'm asking Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- whether the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, the Republic of Serbia, participated in the military operations in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Never did a single police unit as such from Serbia cross the Drina or the Danube, but there were individual policemen who volunteered to participate in the war in order to defend the Serbian people there. These policemen went there as volunteers, and during their absence their employment rights were protected. In Vukovar, there was no police unit, only the 1st Guards Brigade. The Territorial Defence of Vukovar was subordinated to the 1st Guards Brigade. All the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party became members of the 1st Guards Brigade. What police units these are that were allegedly in Vukovar, I don't know. I went to Vukovar twice while the struggle for liberation was going on. I saw everything. I was at the front lines. I visited almost every street. It's impossible that there was something there that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Subparagraph (l), Mr. Seselj, says: "Financed Serb military and police and irregular soldiers in Croatia who perpetrated crimes as specified in this indictment." Let me ask you, then, did the army and police of the Krajina perpetrate crimes, and who on the Serb side perpetrated crimes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb army on the police of the Republika Srpska Krajina or, rather, the previous Serb autonomous provinces, did not perpetrate crimes. Crimes occurred only in individual incidents which were beyond control. As for financing, the authorities in Serbia never financed the military or the police of the Republika Srpska Krajina. They provided financial support to the legal government of the Republika Srpska Krajina. Those lawful authorities, when they received financial assistance, decided what their priorities were in spending that money. I do not exclude that sometimes assistance was provided in the form of equipment or food, but there was no financing of a military or police organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Seselj, what the relationship was between the government in Serbia, the government in Yugoslavia, and the government in Krajina, the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and what their attitude was to the crimes perpetrated by individuals and groups?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three governments were categorically opposed to the commission of crimes, both crimes against prisoners of war and crimes against the civilian population. It was not always possible, however, to prevent the occurrence of crimes. That was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of cases where, for example, Milan Martic, whom you mentioned, personally ordered the arrest of individuals who had committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was in Knin in November 1991 accompanying the minister of justice, I visited the Knin prison. There was some Croatian prisoners of war there. They were all later exchanged. And there was a group of Serbs who had been charged with committing crimes over Croatian civilians. As far as I can remember, in the area of Kordun. They were charged, indicted, and I don't know what happened next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in prison you saw Serbs who had been arrested by Martic's Police - the term used here - because of crimes they had committed against Croats.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assert categorically that in November 1991, they were in the prison in Knin, and this is easy to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. And finally, subparagraph (m), at the end of paragraph 26, it says: "Controlled, contributed to, or otherwise utilised Serbian state-run media outlets to manipulate Serbian public opinion by spreading exaggerated and false messages of ethnically based attacks by Croats against Serb people in order to create an atmosphere of fear and hatred amongst Serbs living in Serbia and Croatia.
