The propaganda generated by the Serbian media was an important tool in contributing to the perpetration of crimes in Croatia." So you heard this whole subparagraph (m). What can you say first of all about the media in Serbia at the time and whether there were opposition papers and TV stations and whether there was freedom of information?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, these are not legal statements. They're political statements. Secondly, Serbia was the first on the territory of the former Yugoslavia to introduce freedom of the press, to begin the privatisation of state-run media, and to give freedom to private media. I know for certain that the state-owned television on more than one occasion refused to broadcast the most terrible documentary footage of crimes perpetrated against civilians, and I know that -- against Serb civilians, and I know that it was the opposition media who were always more critical of the authorities in Croatia than the state-owned media were. That's a fact. In 1991, 1992, there was a huge number of private newspapers, privately owned papers, coming out in Serbia. Many later stopped coming out because there was intense competition. Anyone could publish whatever they wanted to. In that period, no newspaper was banned. As far as I can remember, there was a ban in 1990. There was no book that was banned except for the book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the media in Serbia, let's go one-by-one through these allegations, did they spread, exaggerate, and broadcast false messages of ethnically based attacks by Croats against Serb people, as it says here? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Every attack by a Croat against a Serb was ethnically motivated. Secondly, there were many such attacks. The facts about such attacks were published. It happened sometimes in the Western media that attacks against Serbs and Serb victims were falsely portrayed as attacks by Serbs against Croats and Croat victims. We have a number of examples where Serbs who had been killed were shown on the Western media, especially in Austria and Germany, and they were portrayed as Croatian victims. Sometimes our media would broadcast footage from the foreign media, especially the opposition ones. And then the families of the victims would speak up and say that it was their family members who had been killed and not Croats. There were many such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, did the media, as it says here, and it says especially state-run media in Serbia, did they create an atmosphere of fear and hatred?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to speak about such a generalised allegation. How did they create -- supposedly create this atmosphere of fear and hatred? When we spoke about crimes perpetrated by Croats against Serb civilians, this cannot be described as creating an atmosphere of fear and hatred. This might only be the case had we lied, had we said that the Croats had killed such-and-such a number of Serb civilians and then this was shown to be untrue. But we only had the reverse; Muslims and Croats claiming that their civilians had been killed when this turned out to be a falsehood. The Muslims sometimes killed their own civilians in order to portray these crimes as crimes committed by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you had personal experience of all this, tell us, what was the realistic possibility for the media from Serbia to influence the population in the Krajina? For example, the media from Belgrade influencing people in Glina, Petrinja, Lika, Banja, Kordun?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I travelled there often, I can testify to the fact that the local Serbian population there was very angry because the Serbian media were not broadcasting enough information about all the events there and all their sufferings. And very often you couldn't even see TV Belgrade in the western parts of the country. The Belgrade papers arrived rarely and very late, so they mostly relied on their own media. They had their own radio stations. Sometimes someone would publish a newspaper, but as far as I know there were no daily papers there. These papers were published rarely. So they mainly relied on radio stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The electronic media could not be seen. Some newspapers did arrive, but what was the realistic opportunity for the Croatian media to influence this population?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the population could watch Croatian television, listen to broadcasts by Croatian stations. This only intensified their fear and hatred because in international law hate-speak has never been a crime. It's only been portrayed as a crime here. But you will see that in the Croatian media the hate-speak was far worse and more widespread than in the Serb media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we are now referring to state-run media because the point here was that I utilised state-run media to create an atmosphere of fear and hatred.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The state-run media in Serbia had the most nuanced reports on all the war events. They -- the opposition media followed instructions from foreign intelligence agencies and provided information that was detrimental to the Serb side, but never were any of these media banned, even though it was well known they were receiving money from abroad, and every year in the American Congress there were reports as to how much money the American government was giving for subversive activities on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In the year 2000, this was about $100 million. It's no secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just spoke about the media who were close to the authorities or the media who were close to the opposition. Can you tell us in very general terms what percentage of the media were close to the authorities and what percentage to the opposition?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one media outlet that was close to the authorities. It was the so-called Radio-Television Serbia. It was the only media outlet close to the government. All the other media in Serbia were more or less oppositionist. Television Studio B and Television Politika, all Belgrade newspapers were on the side of opposition. They were all under the umbrella of the Politika publishing house. You remember that in 1992 we wanted to turn Politika company into a public enterprise. However, the opposition was so great we had to abandon the idea. All the newspapers published by the Borba publishing house, including Vecernje Novosti, were on the side of the opposition. There were no state-controlled media apart from the Radio-Television Serbia. Even there, they didn't always listen to the government, but they had a management board that included members of the government but also members of the opposition. I believe Slobodan Rakitic, from the Serbian Renewal Movement, and another two members of the opposition were on that management board. That was much more in terms of opposition representation than they had in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were considered as a hard-line opposition. Were media in Serbia free or not?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were free because there were no bans on newspapers or on books apart from the book The Protocols of Zionist Wisemen. I remember that the police came to seize that book but they didn't have a proper warrant so they only seized only three copies, not the entire circulation. The authorities avoided imposing any bans on the media and I remember that it was a great achievement of the current government compared to the previous period when the regime frequently banned certain books. Under the previous regime, nobody could publish any books on their own, or private newspapers. Somebody tried in 1986, but they were sent to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say that in that entire decade only one book was banned. Why?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was anti-Semitic in content. It had nothing to do with our internal Yugoslavia situation. The Protocols of Zionist Wisemen is a famous book. It dates back to a hundred years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what was the influence of foreign media on the population of the FRY and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were free to watch cable television, choosing their own programmes without any restrictions, and foreign newspapers were freely on sale in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you buy in Belgrade all the leading European newspapers from all the European countries?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally bought Time, NewsWeek magazines, sometimes the Washington Post, sometimes The New York Times, but you could buy the newspapers from all Western countries; American, French, English, Italian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what was the influence of the foreign media on Serbian media?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their influence was great. Many of our opposition media outlets were under the influence of foreign media, such as Studio B. The television of the city of Belgrade was established in 1990 and it acted as an oppositionist television station, and I presented to our parliament reports on how they received equipment from the British embassy as a gift that was recorded. People informed me of those deliveries and I went there to see it with my own eyes and then I reported it to the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we had Stjepan Mesic, among others, here. Do you remember his activities from the time when he was occupying the highest positions in Croatia and in the FRY?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Stipe Mesic was elected president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, the Serb Radical Party held large protest rallies in front of the federal Assembly building sometime in 1991. His election failed in the first attempt because he didn't have enough votes, but then came representatives of the European Community, insisted that he be appointed, and they even attended his election as a form of pressure. I believe the Dutch foreign minister was among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean Mr. Van den Broek?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Stipe Mesic left Belgrade sometime in 1991 and went to the Croatian parliament, saying from the rostrum, "I fulfilled my mission. Yugoslavia exists no more." Those are the historic words of Stipe Mesic. So he became the president of Yugoslavia with a mission to destroy it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you what he said here as a witness. Page 10530 of the transcript. I draw your attention to the fact that we only have an English version of the transcript, and I will quote some passages from his testimony. [In English] "It was those who were attacking and taking place -- taking police stations who, as later become quite evident, were trying to establish the borders of a Greater Serbia running from Virovitica through Karlovac to Karlobag. If you look at all the acts of provocation that took place, they were actually setting up the borders of a Greater Serbia." [Interpretation] That relates to the Serbs in Krajina and the Yugoslav People's Army. Is that correct, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's misusing the ideology of the Serb Radical Party, our ideological concept of Greater Serbia and our idea of the borders Karlovac, Ogulin -- Karlobag, Ogulin, Karlovac, Virovitica, and he also forgets the numbers of Muslims, Albanians, Macedonians and others. For the defence of their freedoms, they led a struggle that has nothing to do with our ideas. God knows whether future generations will manage to fulfil this idea in the Balkans when the Western influences are eliminated. This is a very, very long-term project. I have already mentioned it is more than a -- more than 300 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 10532, Mesic says, and I'm skipping some parts to save time: "[In English] The Serbs in Croatia were tricked because Milosevic had told them that the Serbs would live together in a single state and that this was their right because they had the right to self-determination. He was deceiving the world because he was saying that he was fighting for Yugoslavia. However, he was doing everything to destroy it." [Interpretation] So Mesic is saying that I did everything to break up Yugoslavia. And he is the same man who said that his mission was accomplished and that Yugoslavia was no more.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were one of the rare presidents of any federal unit who struggled for the preservation of Yugoslavia. Second, you could not trick the Serbs of Krajina because they couldn't be tricked by anyone. Third, your policies were always more moderate than those of the Serbs in Krajina, and you even clashed with some of their governments over that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And fourth, nobody could raise the Serb people in Krajina to an armed insurgency and to fight the Tudjman regime if their lives had not been in danger, if their very survival had not been threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, we are coming to a subject that you as a politician, as an oppositionist politician, have to be familiar with. Look at what Mesic says concerning the Serbian Democratic Party. It's on the same page, 10532. "[In English] At the beginning when the SDS was being set up, it did not appear that that party would become too radical. It was to struggle for cultural autonomy. But as time went on, it became evident that this party was being manipulated by Belgrade, which means the regime of Slobodan Milosevic and he himself, and that they were doing only things that would lead to the creation of a Greater Serbia, an ethnically pure territory cleansed of the non-Serbian population. "In areas where the SDS took power, the population was completely cleansed, that is, the non-Serbian population. This was an organisation that was to bring a dowry to Greater Serbia in the form of new territories." [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you've just heard what Mr. Mesic had stated here. According to him, I manipulated the Serbian Democratic Party in Krajina, and in those places where they took over power, they carried out an ethnic cleansing of non-Serbs in order to create new territories for Serbs, pure territories.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible for you to manipulate the SDS because the leadership of the SDS, especially Jovan Raskovic as its first president, were not in collusion with you and had no contact with you. They were in collusion and in contact with the leading opposition leaders in Belgrade. They had been so since before the war. Jovan Raskovic and another number of Serbs from Croatia kept company exclusively with Dobrica Cosic, myself, and other opposition leaders. I met Jovan Raskovic at Dobrica Cosic's place, and we met to talk, to criticise the regime and share opinions. They could not have been close to you; they were close to the opposition. That's how these three parties came into being, the Serbian Democratic Party in Croatia, the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the DS in Serbia, the Democratic Party in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Mesic's claim that they acted as Serb agents, promoting Serbian interests?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mesic is right about one thing: The Serbian Democratic Party did insist on cultural autonomy, but look at this fact: At the first multi-party elections in Croatia the majority of Serbian people did not vote for the Serbian Democratic Party, they voted for Racan's party, the Party of Democratic Changes, which was made up mostly of Croats. Serbs were very disappointed by the victory of Franjo Tudjman and the Croatian Democratic Union who were obviously Ustashas, because they had brought back notorious Ustashas back to the country and given some of them ministerial positions, and Serbs understood clearly that they had to rally together to protect themselves. They did not wish for any autonomy in that Croatia as a state of citizens. But when they realised that the Ustasha regime was being restored in Croatia, a regime that openly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Seselj, very specifically: Were they trying to ensure some new territories for Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were trying to protect their lives. And Jovan Raskovic openly made it known that if Croatia remains in Yugoslavia, they didn't want any territorial autonomy. They wanted only cultural autonomy. They wanted to have the right to have their own language, customs, traditions, et cetera. If Croatia wanted a confederation, then they would be asking for territorial autonomy within in Croatia for Serbs. And only in the event of Croatian secession they wanted the right to self-determination. They wanted to remain within Yugoslavia. I wish to remind you that international -- in international legal practice, federal units did not have the right to self-determination. Only peoples or nations had that right. And it was considered that that right had been exercised once and for all with the creation of Yugoslavia as a federal state after the First World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. I will now ask you a question that is closely related to the passage from that Croatian paper we quoted a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm sorry to interrupt you but there is another case here this afternoon at 2.15, and we have to adjourn. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 31st day of August, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
